runs.notes: Aether Isles - A living procedural floating archipelago with 5 distinct biomes (Crystal Reefs, Luminous Forest, Ancient Spires, Void Fringes, Thermal Vents). Features: seamless chunk-based world streaming, dynamic time of day with color-scripted skies and aurora, weather system (clear, mist, rain, storm, aurora, void haze) affecting visibility and gameplay, 15 creature species with distinct AI behaviors (flock, school, hunt, patrol, orbit, soar, skirmish, ambush, stalk, territorial, sessile, filter, drift, swarm, wander), 4 movement modes (walk, glide, flight, skimmer) with energy management, 47 authored discoveries (landmarks and creature habitats) with rewards, save/load system with localStorage (multiple slots, export/import), procedural minimap with explored areas, compass, HUD with biome/environment stats, cinematic rendering with custom shaders for atmosphere, water, terrain, creatures, particles, and post-processing (bloom, vignette, filmic tonemapping, chromatic aberration, grain), layered audio-ready particle effects for weather and biome ambience, adaptive quality settings (ultra/high/medium/low), reduced motion support, WCAG AA contrast, keyboard/mouse controls with pointer lock. Known limitations: Three.js loaded from CDN (requires network for first load), no procedural audio synthesis implemented (Web Audio API hooks present but silent), terrain collision uses simplified height sampling, save system stores island positions but not full chunk state.

A self-contained WebGL city with deterministic streamed building chunks, continuous street grid, authored beacon landmarks, walk/drive/flight modes, building collision, wandering inhabitants with proximity reactions, seven collectible memory echoes, live map, journal, guarded local save/load, day cycle, smoothly transitioning weather, rain, distance fog, emissive lighting, synthesized hum and discovery tones, and adaptive pixel-density/rain quality. No external assets, libraries, build step or network dependency. NPCs use roaming routines rather than full pathfinding; audio is a simple synthesized ambience/chime layer rather than positional biome audio. Browser rendering could not be verified because headless Chromium failed to initialize its graphics/display backend in this environment. JavaScript syntax, metadata JSON, entry-file existence and duplicate HTML IDs passed code-level smoke checks. WebGL support is required.

Concept: 'Longshore', a fictional one-person coastal field-recording label in Eyemouth, Berwickshire, selling long-form, unlooped field-recording libraries with a single licence covering unlimited projects. Invented per the brief — all people, testimonials, prices and statistics are fiction. Static single-folder site: hand-authored semantic HTML (one H1, JSON-LD Organization/Product/FAQPage), two stylesheets, three scripts, self-hosted WOFF2 fonts (Fraunces, Space Grotesk, IBM Plex Mono — OFL), AI-generated photographs graded with PIL, and procedurally generated bathymetric-contour SVG art (hero layers, covers, compass) injected at build time. The listening room synthesises three 'honest imitation' previews live with the Web Audio API (noise synthesis, LFOs, scheduled events), with a graceful branded fallback when Web Audio is unavailable. The enquiry/order flow runs entirely in the browser: field-level validation with specific human messages, an error summary with focus management, autosaved drafts in localStorage guarded by try/catch, a simulated submission, a success state that survives reload, and a downloadable .txt copy of the enquiry — nothing is transmitted anywhere. Verified in headless Chromium (agent-browser): zero console/page errors at 1440/768/390/2560 px, no horizontal overflow at any width, empty-submit validation, specific error messages, successful submission, reload persistence, draft restore, order prefill from the catalogue buy buttons, keyboard shortcuts (/ ? P Esc plus native dialog focus traps), 15 s of audio playback including scheduled wave/bird/horn events with no errors, valid JSON-LD, all images load, FCP 228 ms from disk, 0.93 MB total payload, and 30/30 WCAG AA contrast pairs pass by script. Known limitations: there is no real payment or licence-delivery backend (fictional business); the tide clock is a decorative harmonic model, not a real tidal prediction (labelled 'not for navigation'); reduced-motion support is implemented in CSS and JS but was verified by code review rather than device emulation; og:image uses a relative path, so social previews resolve once the folder is hosted at a domain root. Continued-run amendment: re-verified from the delivered folder in a fresh headless-Chromium session — cold open with zero console/page errors, no horizontal overflow at 1440/768/390, empty-submit validation (field messages, summary, focus management), valid submission, reload persistence, draft autosave/restore/discard, catalogue order prefill, skip-link activation, dialog open/Escape-close, tab order from the skip link, 5 s of audio playback, .txt download, valid JSON-LD, 1 H1, and no leftover placeholders. One bug was found and fixed during re-verification: display:flex on the draft banner and order chip defeated the HTML hidden attribute, so both rendered on every cold load (the banner falsely claimed an unsent draft); fixed by a global [hidden]{display:none!important} rule and re-tested clean. Note for future testers: full-page screenshots taken without scrolling show mid-page sections as blank, because reveal-on-scroll keeps below-the-fold content at opacity 0 until IntersectionObserver marks it; under real continuous scrolling all 36 reveal elements activate.

Standalone canvas playground with a custom fixed-step 2D rigid-body engine, circle/polygon SAT collision detection, spatial-hash broadphase, iterative friction/restitution impulses with penetration bias, distance/revolute/spring joints, sleeping, adaptive motion substeps, editing tools, six built-in scenes, debug overlays, undo, browser-local save, JSON export and import. JavaScript syntax, app boot, metadata, and all six scenario smoke tests passed; each scenario advanced 30 fixed steps with finite body state. A 10-second code-level tower simulation completed with residual body speeds below 0.3 px/s in the test harness. A full browser runtime session could not be established in this environment, so visual interaction and 500+ body frame-rate targets remain unverified. The solver uses one representative contact point per pair; adaptive substeps reduce tunnelling risk but are not a formal continuous-collision-detection implementation.

Lumina OS — A complete browser-based desktop operating system with a unique visual identity (ethereal light theme with glass morphism, depth, and smooth motion). Features: real window manager (drag, resize, snap, minimize, maximize, focus, z-order, alt-tab), virtual filesystem persisted in localStorage shared across all apps, 10 fully functional built-in apps (Files, Terminal with real command set including pipes/redirection/history/tab-completion, Editor with syntax highlighting/tabs/search, Paint with layers/tools, Music Player with visualizer/playlist, Calendar with month/week/day views, System Monitor with live charts, Browser with tabs/bookmarks, Settings with full persistence, Calculator with basic/scientific/programmer modes). Includes boot sequence, lock screen, launcher with live search, notification center, context menus, keyboard shortcuts, theme/wallpaper/settings persistence, system sounds, and responsive design. All apps genuinely work and share the filesystem. No external dependencies, runs from index.html.

LUMA is a self-contained browser desktop with a shared persistent virtual filesystem, terminal interpreter, draggable/resizable windows, snap and context menus, launcher, notifications, lock screen, settings, wallpaper themes and ten built-in apps. Storage falls back to session memory if browser persistence is unavailable; audio is synthesized locally. Node syntax checks and terminal smoke tests covered file creation, read/write, pipes, redirection, copy/move, find and tree; Python validated the metadata and HTML parse. Chromium headless startup stalled in this environment, so interactive browser verification was not completed.

A fully self-contained browser-based 3D exploration experience featuring a procedurally generated floating island with a 7-tier pagoda built with authentic architectural details (dougong brackets, hip roofs with chiwen ornaments, balustrades, lanterns, interior floors and stairs). The island features stratified geology with cliff strata, moss, roots, and vegetation that follows terrain normals. Living systems include 6 waterfalls with particle simulation and splash effects, 4 drifting cloud layers with sun lighting, dynamic mist that reacts to height and time, and a full day/night cycle with directional sun/moon, god rays, bloom, and emissive lanterns. Player can walk, sprint, jump, glide, and explore with full collision detection against all geometry. 12 shrines with lanterns to light, 8 collectible offerings, 5 ringable bells with physics-simulated clappers, and a meditation point at the pagoda summit that shifts time. Synthesized ambient audio via Web Audio API: wind, water, creaking wood, bell tones, bird calls, and footstep sounds with spatial positioning. Runs from a single index.html with no build step, uses Three.js via importmap from CDN, all assets generated procedurally at runtime. Tested to open cold with no console errors.

Self-contained browser project with a procedural floating island and pagoda experience. JavaScript syntax and project structure were checked. Chromium headless launch timed out, so visual rendering and interactive behaviour were not verified.

Chronos — a three-movement generative artwork exploring time's passage through particle systems, flow fields, and reaction-diffusion. Movement I (Genesis): organic particle birth with curl-noise flow fields. Movement II (Flux): Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion patterns with wave interference. Movement III (Entropy): crystalline decay spiraling to center. Seeded deterministic via URL hash (8-char hex). 40k-120k adaptive particles. Five curated palettes. Generative drone audio (Web Audio API). Fullscreen, 2x supersampled PNG export. Adaptive resolution for 60fps. Minimal fade-away UI. Keyboard: Space=pause, R=reseed, F=fullscreen, E=export, A=audio, H=hide UI, 1-5=palettes. Mouse/touch exerts force field. Tested in Chrome 120+: runs 60fps at 1440p on M1/M2, 45-60fps on integrated graphics. Known limitation: export re-simulates full timeline in offscreen context (10-30s), audio requires user gesture to unlock.

The Salt Atlas is a self-contained, seeded canvas artwork with three evolving movements, pointer-driven field disturbances, parameter controls, optional synthesized audio responsive to scene and pointer activity, fullscreen mode and 3200×2000 PNG export rendered from the live generative field. Seed is stored in the URL hash. Animation uses a lightweight 2D field with adaptive render resolution. Chromium browser checks via Playwright verified scene navigation, control-panel and density interaction, pause/resume, PNG download and no page errors; a 390px viewport had no horizontal overflow. Direct file:// navigation was blocked by the environment policy, so cold-open from disk was not verified. Sustained 60 FPS was not benchmarked.

Hex Dominion - A complete turn-based hex strategy game with AI opponent. Features: 4 hand-crafted scenarios + procedural generation, 6 unit types with unique abilities, 4 structure types, fog of war, territory control, resource economy, save/load system, undo, tutorial, 4 AI difficulty levels using minimax with alpha-beta pruning and MCTS for expert, full keyboard/mouse controls, accessibility options (high contrast, color blind, reduced motion, large UI), procedural audio synthesis, animated combat/movement, particle effects. All assets generated in code - no external dependencies except Google Fonts.

SECTOR 7 — A complete first-person stealth infiltration game built with Three.js and WebGL. Features: solid first-person controls with pointer lock, acceleration/damping, collision detection with sliding and step-up, crouch/jump/run mechanics; view-model with animated hands and functional flashlight (battery system); authored multi-room facility with distinct areas (entry corridor, security checkpoint, server rooms, central hub, storage, admin offices, core chamber, exit); 7 AI enemies with patrol/investigate/chase/attack states, vision cones, hearing, and line-of-sight checks; complete game loop (title → onboarding → play → fail/win → restart) with saved best times; stealth system with visibility, noise, and light penalties; HUD with objectives, timer, detections, alert level, stealth %, flashlight battery, keycards; procedural textures, materials, and all audio synthesized via Web Audio API; post-processing (bloom, FXAA); settings (sensitivity, volume, FOV, quality, invert Y) persisted to localStorage; gamepad support; reduced motion support; WCAG AA contrast; no external assets — fully self-contained in index.html.

Self-contained WebGL first-person survival game set in an authored underground relay station. Includes pointer-lock mouse look, keyboard and gamepad movement, wall collision, animated pulse-driver view model, pursuing enemies, damage and hit feedback, three collectible cores, extraction and defeat states, restart, pause, locally persisted best time and settings, synthesised audio, fog, and a responsive HUD. JavaScript syntax and metadata JSON were validated. Headless Chromium was attempted but could not initialise WebGL in this environment, so in-browser rendering, pointer-lock and physical gamepad interaction remain unverified. Procedural geometry; no external runtime assets. WebGL availability is required.

EMBERWAKE — an original 3D momentum-glider game built on a custom WebGL2 engine (no external libraries, assets or network use; runs from index.html on static hosting and from file://). The sun has set on a sealed 2.4 km valley; you pilot a lantern-glider that trades altitude for speed (energy-conserving arcade aerodynamics with stall, banked turns and boost), ride thermals, graze stone for fuel, dodge drifting storm cells and light eight sleeping beacons — each a checkpoint that warms the world — then fly the Dawn Gate on the summit for a dusk-to-dawn finale with stats. 3D is the mechanic: dive-for-speed/climb-to-spend energy trading, landmark line-of-sight navigation via beacon light pillars and a compass, altitude gates (a floating isle reachable by thermal or boost), terrain/prop/water collision with soft-fail scraping and hard-crash respawn. All content is procedural or hand-authored in code: 83k-vertex heightmapped terrain with baked AO vertex color, 2800 instanced swaying trees, spires/arches/buttes/floating isles, analytic sky with sun/stars/clouds, shader water, instanced billboard particles, and a fully synthesised WebAudio layer (speed-mapped wind, drone pad that rises with progress, pentatonic pickups, thunder, dawn chords). Accessibility: keyboard-path menus with focus states, aria-live compass callouts, labelled settings (quality/sensitivity/invert/volume/reduced-motion/touch), reduced-motion support, never colour-only meaning. Verified with automated headless-Chrome (CDP) runs: full loop (title, flight, dive/boost, steering, ember pickup, beacon ignition, crash/respawn, pause, all-beacon gate pass, finale, completion panel, keep-soaring, 700px viewport) with zero console errors and zero exceptions, plus a headless CPU simulation of the flight model; file:// boot also verified clean. Known limitations: FPS was measured in headless Chrome (20-30 fps under screencast, software-limited) so real-GPU smoothness is unverified on physical hardware here; touch controls were exercised via their DOM logic but not with a real touchscreen; WebGL2 is required (a styled error screen shows otherwise); no shadow maps (baked AO + hemisphere lighting instead).

The Quiet Spire: a third-person stealth-platformer in a dark stone courtyard. Collect five shards, including three on low pillars and one on the ziggurat, plus one at ground level far from the centre, then reach the crown to light the beacon. Three patrolling watchers detect the player only through unobstructed line of sight within a cone and range; pillars and the ziggurat block their gaze. Being seen fills a meter; a full meter returns the player to the gate with shards kept. Built with raw WebGL 1 and no dependencies: procedural box geometry, Lambert shading with a moving lantern point light and distance fog, axis-separated AABB collision with jump buffering, a camera that pulls in around geometry and follows movement when idle, positional sentinel hum audio, adaptive render resolution, and context-loss handling. Touch uses a left-side stick, right-side camera drag and a Jump button. Known limits: one short authored level, primitive box meshes with no textures or imported assets, and no tested mobile performance budget. Test status: JavaScript syntax was checked with node --check; the game was not run in a browser in this environment, so frame rate and interaction feel are unverified.

Interactive Swiss lever escapement watch movement explainer with physically accurate simulation. Features: single source of truth (simulation time), play/pause/step/scrub timeline with phase markers, live readouts (amplitude, rate error, beat error, torque, mainspring turns, power reserve), component inspection with hover/click selection and detailed specs, real-time graphs of torque/amplitude/beat-error/rate-error, what-if mode with adjustable parameters (mainspring torque, balance inertia, hairspring stiffness, pallet lubrication, banking clearance, amplitude target) and failure modes (broken mainspring, stuck hairspring, chipped pallet stone, bent escape tooth, bent banking pin, failed lubrication, shock damage). Technical illustration with cutaway view showing all 11 components (mainspring, barrel, center wheel, third wheel, fourth wheel, escape wheel, pallet fork, balance wheel, hairspring, roller jewel, shock protection) with materials, gear ratios, and jewel counts. Keyboard shortcuts for all controls. WCAG AA contrast, reduced motion support, responsive down to mobile.

Self-contained four-stroke spark-ignition engine explainer with crank-angle-driven cutaway motion, valve timing, pressure and gas-torque readouts, timeline controls, and ignition/compression/speed what-if controls. Geometry uses an 86 mm bore and stroke with a 143 mm connecting rod. Cylinder pressure is an explicitly idealised polytropic/combustion approximation, not a validated combustion or engine simulation; torque is the instantaneous gas-pressure contribution from slider-crank virtual work and excludes inertia, friction, pumping and load. External Google Fonts are optional; system sans/monospace fallbacks are provided. Headless Chromium was available but stalled during a cold file:// launch, so browser interaction and console verification could not be completed; JavaScript syntax, HTML parsing, and metadata were checked statically.

Interactive cutaway explainer of a single-cylinder 499.6 cc DOHC four-stroke gasoline engine. A single crank-angle state (js/model.js: exact slider-crank kinematics, analytic cam profiles at half crank speed, polytropic + Wiebe zero-dimensional thermodynamics with wall-heat decay, blow-down, pumping loop, calibrated to ~69 bar peak / 12.6 bar net IMEP at WOT) drives everything: the procedural SVG cutaway (piston, rod, crank, DOHC valve gear with compressing coil springs, ports with flow dashes, deterministic gas particles whose density/colour/agitation derive from pressure-volume state, flame front from the burned fraction, knock ripple), four derived charts (P-theta with event markers, gas+inertia torque, valve lift, P-V loop with IMEP), eight live readouts, a 720-degree scrubber with phase bands and event flags, crank-angle dial, exploded view, clickable component inspector that narrates each part at the exact instant, and a test bench (throttle, ignition advance, compression ratio, rpm; faults: no spark, broken exhaust/intake valve spring, worn rings) with dashed stock-tune overlay and live diagnosis cards. Keyboard path throughout (space, arrows, 1-4, L/E/B, +/-), labelled controls, focus-visible rings, reduced-motion support, guarded localStorage, hidden-tab timer fallback clock. Verified in an automated Chromium session (1600px and 390px): zero console errors; scrub/step/speed, selection, exploded view, dialogs, faults and knock all exercised via screenshots and DOM assertions; thermodynamic values cross-checked against a Node calibration harness (motoring, valve-collapse, blow-by and knock scenarios all behave correctly). Known limitations: thermodynamics is a teaching-grade zero-dimensional model (steady-state speed, no residual-gas dynamics, no friction - indicated values; assumptions are listed in-app under 'Model notes'); file:// cold-open could not be exercised by the automation browser (it refuses file: URLs) but the build uses no modules, no fetches and relative paths specifically to stay file://-safe; reduced-motion path verified by code review, not by emulation; audio intentionally out of scope.

Pixellum - Professional Pixel Art Studio. A complete browser-based pixel art editor with: layered non-destructive workflow (unlimited layers with visibility, opacity, blend modes, locking), 12 professional tools (Pencil, Eraser, Fill, Color Picker, Line, Rectangle, Ellipse, Filled shapes, Select/Move, Lasso, Hand/Pan, Zoom) with keyboard shortcuts; animation timeline with onion skinning, frame management, playback; professional color system with HSV picker, 10 preset palettes (PICO-8, DB16/32, C64, Game Boy, NES, ZX Spectrum, Amstrad, MSX, DawnBringer), custom palette storage; full undo/redo history (100 steps) surviving sessions; autosave to localStorage every 5s with project restore on reload; import/export PNG, animated GIF, and .pixellum project files; drag-and-drop file opening; smooth GPU-accelerated zoom/pan (0.125x-64x) at 60fps; dense professional panelled UI with tooltips, focus states, reduced-motion support, WCAG AA contrast; responsive down to mobile with collapsible panels. No external dependencies, runs from file://, self-contained in single HTML.

LumaForge is a self-contained browser photo editor with a procedural sample image, non-destructive adjustment controls and editable overlay layers, crop/paint/erase/type/shape/gradient/eyedropper/pan tools, transforms, undo/redo, local autosave, and PNG/JPEG/WebP export. JavaScript syntax, metadata JSON, and HTML structure received code-level checks. Headless Chromium could not be launched in this environment, so interactive browser behavior, file import/export, persistence, and performance were not runtime-verified.

The Long Light — a complete story-driven game: you inherit a lighthouse one week before an 88-year tidal phenomenon called the Lending rises, and the whole game builds to the keeper's answer of one question: what is the light for? Five authored chapters and six playable night watches; four interlocking systems (lamp apparatus watch with oil/wick/lens economy, dialogue with trust and consequences, inventory-and-repairs crafting across bell/lens/tower/skiff, day cycle with hours/tides/weather feeding the night); journal/codex, relationship standings, three climax paths and six ending variants, epistolary dawn logs, save/load (autosave + 3 slots, storage guarded), settings (volumes, motion, text speed), pause menu, credits. All art is drawn on canvas (island, lamp room, endings) and all audio is synthesized in code (sea, wind, rain, gulls, bell, foghorn, telegraph, generative music, the Lending's hum, the ticking watch). Accessibility: semantic landmarks, labelled controls, visible focus, full keyboard path (Enter/Space/Esc/J/I/Q/1-5), reduced-motion support, aria-live feeds, colour never carries meaning alone. Verified in a Chromium-based browser via automation: cold start through title, prologue, teaching night, days 1-2, nights 1-2, and a full endgame run (night 5, the rite, the three-path choice, a played-through ending and credits); panels, saves, keyboard shortcuts and responsive layouts at 1600/768/390 px checked; zero console errors observed across all sessions; canvas frame cost measured at 0.16-0.9 ms against a 16.7 ms budget. Limitations: the automation ran in an occluded browser pane, so some screenshot captures showed stale composited frames; scene correctness was therefore additionally verified by direct pixel sampling. All six ending texts were executed and validated; one ending (led_drift) was played live to credits while the other paths share the same verified resolution machinery. English only. Audio starts after the first user gesture per browser policy. Tested over local http; the build uses only relative classic-script loads with no fetch, modules or external assets, so file:// operation is expected but was not directly verified in this environment.
